hero.title: The Terminal
hero.subtitle: The terminal is an old but very powerful tool for your computer.

lead.paragraph1: Behind every app there are text commands. The terminal is a program where you type commands. You can control your computer very precisely with it.
lead.paragraph2: You do not need any experience. At the end you will know: What is a graphical interface? What is a command line? How do file addresses work? And you will know the most important commands.

guiCli.title: Two Ways to Use Your Computer
guiCli.analogy: A GUI is like a map. You tap on places and get guided there. A CLI is like an address. You type the address and go directly to the destination. You can also give the same address to many taxis.
guiCli.scientific: GUI means: Graphical User Interface. You click on windows, icons, and buttons. CLI means: Command-Line Interface. You type commands as text. The terminal is the program with the text window. The shell is the program inside it that understands your commands.
guiCli.analogyBreak: This comparison has limits: a wrong command can cause much more damage than a wrong address.
guiCli.history: Command lines have existed since the 1960s. Graphical interfaces came in the 1980s. The command line came first.
guiCli.renameExample: Example: Rename 500 photos. With a GUI you have to click each photo one by one. With the command line you can do it with one single command.

comparison.guiResult: You see pictures and buttons. Easy to learn. Good for editing images. Hard to automate.
comparison.cliResult: You type commands as text. Very precise. Good for automation. You need to learn the commands.

terminalChoice.title: Which Terminal to Use?
terminalChoice.text: Mac and Linux have a terminal built in. On Windows, use Windows Terminal or WSL. Tip: Programs like VS Code also have a built-in terminal.

noUndo.title: There Is No Undo in the Terminal
noUndo.text: The terminal has no recycle bin. A command runs immediately. Start with safe commands like pwd and ls. They only show information and do not change anything.

paths.title: Paths — Where Am I?
paths.analogy: Think of an office building. An absolute path is the full address: Building, Floor 3, Room 312. A relative path says: Go one door to the left. The working directory is the room you are standing in right now.
paths.scientific: A path is the address of a file. An absolute path starts at the very top of the file system, for example /home/user/file.txt. A relative path starts from your current folder. A dot . means: here. Two dots .. mean: one level up.
paths.analogyBreak: This comparison has limits: in a file system there are shortcuts that do not exist in a real building.
paths.crossPlatform: On Linux and Mac you use / as separator. On Windows you use \. Most programs understand both.

walkthrough.title: Exercise: Navigate the File System
walkthrough.step1: pwd → Shows you where you are
walkthrough.step2: mkdir project → Creates a new folder
walkthrough.step3: cd project → Goes into the folder
walkthrough.step4: mkdir data src → Creates two folders at once
walkthrough.step5: cd data → Goes into the data folder

pitfalls.title: Common Mistakes with Paths
pitfalls.text: Folder names with spaces need quotes: cd "My Folder". Use pwd often so you know where you are.

resolver.title: Try it: where does the path land?
resolver.intro: A path depends on 2 things: Where are you standing? And what do you type? Change one of them below. Then you see at once: the path leads somewhere else.

commands.title: Your First Commands
commands.intro: These 9 commands are like 9 words in a foreign language. You will not be perfect, but you can get by.
commands.tabCompletion: Tip: Type the first few letters and press the Tab key. The terminal completes the name for you.

miniProject.title: Exercise: Build a Project Folder
miniProject.step1: mkdir ai-project → Creates the main folder
miniProject.step3: mkdir data src docs → Creates three subfolders
miniProject.step4: touch requirements.txt README.md → Creates two files
miniProject.step5: ls → Shows all files and folders
miniProject.step6: cp requirements.txt backup.txt → Copies the file
miniProject.step7: mv README.md docs/ → Moves the file into the docs folder

rmWarning.title: Careful: rm Deletes Forever
rmWarning.text: The rm command deletes files permanently. There is no recycle bin.
rmWarning.tip: Tip: Use rm -i. Then you will be asked before each deletion. Always check with pwd and ls that you are in the right folder.

commands.forwardLink: In the next article you will learn about your development environment. That is where you write your programs. After that you will learn Git.

flags.title: More About Flags
flags.intro: Flags change what a command does. They start with a dash. For example: ls -l shows more details. ls -a shows hidden files.
flags.examples: You can combine flags: ls -la shows hidden files with details.
flags.help: Type --help after a command to see which flags exist. For example: ls --help.

aiTerminal.title: Why the Terminal Matters for AI
aiTerminal.intro: Many AI computers have no graphical interface. You connect to them through the terminal.
aiTerminal.useCases: You install programs with pip and conda. You start AI training with a command. And automatic tests also run in the terminal.

items.guiCli: A GUI has pictures and buttons. A CLI has text commands. Both are useful.
items.paths: Every file has an address. That is the path. There are absolute and relative paths.
items.commands: 9 commands are enough to start: pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, touch, cat, cp, mv, rm.
items.tabCompletion: The Tab key completes file names automatically.
items.noUndo: The terminal has no undo. The rm command deletes forever.

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint
checkpoint.item1: When is a GUI better? When is a CLI? Give two examples for each.
checkpoint.item2: You are in the folder /home/user/project. How do you get to /home/user/data/file.csv?
checkpoint.item3: Create a folder, put a file in it, and check if it is there. Which commands do you need?

q1.question: What is the difference between GUI and CLI?
q1.b: A GUI has pictures and buttons. A CLI has text commands.
q1.c: A CLI only works on Linux
q1.d: A GUI is for professionals. A CLI is for beginners.
q1.explanation: A GUI shows windows, icons, and buttons. A CLI works with text. Both are useful.

q2.question: You are in the folder /home/user/project/data. What does cd .. do?
q2.explanation: Two dots .. mean: one level up. From /home/user/project/data, cd .. goes to /home/user/project.

q3.question: You want to create a folder "test", put a file "log.txt" inside, and check if it is there. What is the right order?
q3.b: mkdir test, cd test, touch log.txt, ls
q3.c: cd test, mkdir test, touch log.txt
q3.explanation: First create the folder (mkdir test). Then go inside (cd test). Then create the file (touch log.txt). Then check (ls).

q4.question: Why is the command line better for renaming 500 files?
q4.b: One command can rename all 500 files at once
q4.d: The command line has a recycle bin
q4.explanation: The command line can automate: One command renames all 500 files in seconds. In a GUI you have to click each file one by one.

enrichment.intro: Test what you know about terminal commands. Click a card to see the answer. Shuffle and try to explain each command before flipping.

1.back: Shows the full path of your current folder. Always check before deleting files.
1.backExample: Always run pwd before rm. This keeps you safe.

2.back: Lists files and folders. Use -l for details. Use -a for hidden files.
2.backExample: ls -la also shows hidden files like .gitignore.

3.back: Changes your folder. Use cd .. to go up one level. Use cd ~ to go home.
3.backExample: cd alone takes you to your home folder.

4.back: Makes one or more new folders. You can make many at once.
4.backFormula:
mkdir data src docs
mkdir -p parent/child/grandchild
4.backExample: mkdir -p also creates parent folders if needed.

5.back: Prints the whole file to the screen. Good for short files like config files.
5.backExample: For long files use less instead of cat.

6.back: Copies files or folders. For folders with content use -r (recursive).
6.backFormula:
cp file.txt backup.txt
cp -r folder/ copy/
6.backExample: Make a backup before risky changes.

7.back: Moves files to a new place. Also renames them. The command just changes the path.
7.backFormula:
mv old.txt new.txt
mv file.txt folder/
7.backExample: A loop with mv renames 500 files in seconds.

8.back: Deletes files for good. No trash bin. No undo. Use -r for folders. Be very careful.
8.backFormula:
rm file.txt
rm -r folder/
rm -i file.txt  # asks first
8.backExample: Tip: rm -i asks you before each deletion.
